reels.title: The stockroom and the shop floor

beats.say: Why does a shop keep a tidy stockroom and also a neat shelf out front? Because storing things and finding things are different jobs.
The stockroom is built for careful updates. Every item has one home, so when a price changes, you fix it in one place. That is the app's database.
The shop floor is built for browsing. Similar things sit together with labels, even if that means copies. That is the warehouse, made to answer questions fast.
A data model is the plan for both. It decides what one row means and how tables connect. Without it, everyone reorganises the shelves their own way, and the answers disagree.

check.q: What is a data model mainly for?
opts: Deciding what a row means, how tables connect and how history is kept
check.why: A model is the shared plan for meaning, connections and history, so everyone gets the same answers.

work: Pick one report and write down, in one sentence, what one row of its main table means.
Ask two analysts to compute the same metric and compare results.

reels.title: Normalised in the app, dimensional in the warehouse

beats.say: Why does a city name sit in one table in the app, but get repeated across millions of trips in the warehouse?
In the app, third normal form stores every fact once. The city name lives in a cities table. Rename a city and you change one row, so nothing can disagree.
But analytics reads far more than it writes. Joining ten tables across a billion trips is slow and costly, because every join shuffles data between machines.

So the warehouse denormalises. A fact trip table holds one row per trip, with keys to rider, city and date dimensions. Repeating context on purpose means one join, not ten. Writes are big batch appends, so extra copies are cheap to keep.

check.q: Why does a warehouse deliberately repeat context such as city name?
opts: Because storage is impossible to save
Because reads dominate and fewer joins make scans cheaper and simpler
Because normal forms are illegal in analytics
check.why: Analytics is read heavy and batch loaded, so repeating context avoids costly joins without the update risk an app would face.

work: Take one slow query with many joins and sketch the star that would replace it.
Count joins in your top five dashboards' queries.

reels.title: Anomalies, normal forms and drifting copies

beats.say: If repeating data is fine in a warehouse, what exactly goes wrong when you repeat it in an app?
Update anomalies. Say the city name is copied onto ten thousand trips. Rename it, and a crash halfway leaves some rows old and some new. Now two reports disagree.
The normal forms are the guard. First form bans lists inside a column. Second says every column depends on the whole key. Third says no column depends on another non-key column.
The catch in analytics is that copies can drift too. So load denormalised tables from one source in a single batch job, never edit them by hand, and rebuild when a dimension changes.

check.q: Which problem is third normal form designed to prevent?
opts: A column depending on another non-key column, causing inconsistent copies
Missing indexes on the fact table
check.why: 3NF keeps facts like city name in one place, so an update cannot leave contradictory copies.

work: Find a denormalised column in your warehouse and name the single source that feeds it.
Check that nobody has write access to modelled tables outside the pipeline.

reels.title: When not to model dimensionally

beats.say: When is a dimensional model the wrong choice?
Anything that needs many small, consistent updates, like taking payments. Warehouses are built for scans, not single row writes, so keep that work in a normalised operational database.
Be careful with one wide table for everything. It is cheap to query but hard to govern. Change one definition and you rebuild the whole thing, and columns nobody owns pile up.
Choose by cost. Storage is cheap, joins and rescans are not. Pick stars for broad analyst use, wide tables for one hot dashboard, and keep the raw normalised copy as your source of truth.

check.q: Which workload should stay in a normalised operational database rather than a star schema?
check.why: Warehouses favour big scans and batch appends; frequent single row updates need transactional, normalised storage.

work: List each table in your platform as read heavy or write heavy and check it sits in the right system.
Review any wide table for an owner and a rebuild cost.

reels.title: Model for who reads it

beats.say: Who will read this data? The answer changes the model.

Analysts want simple stars with clear names. Engineers want reliable building blocks to reuse. Machine learning engineers need point in time correct features, meaning values as they were then, not today, or the model cheats by peeking at the future.
Executives want a few trusted metrics with one definition. Language models want a small, well described semantic layer, because they guess wrong when faced with hundreds of cryptic columns.
So one source can feed several models. Build layers: raw, then a reusable core, then marts shaped for each consumer.

check.q: Why do ML features need to be point in time correct?
opts: To avoid training on information from the future
check.why: Using today's values for a past event leaks future information, making the model look better in training than in production.

work: For your top three tables, write the primary consumer and what they need.
Add plain-language descriptions to the columns an LLM or executive would touch.

reels.title: Passports and national IDs

beats.say: A rider moves from Pune to Mumbai. Which city should last year's trips show? Pune, of course. But how does the data remember that?

show.sub: Last year's trips should still say Pune

beats.say: Think of a national ID number. It comes from outside, and it never changes. In data, that is the natural key, like rider id.

Now think of passports. Each renewal gets a new passport number, with the new address. That number belongs to one version of you. In data, that is a surrogate key, made by the warehouse, one per version.
A receipt from last year points at the old passport, so it still shows Pune. New receipts point at the new one. History stays true.

check.q: In the passport analogy, what is the surrogate key?
opts: The passport number for one version of you
check.why: A surrogate key is made by the warehouse and identifies one version of a row. The national ID is the natural key.

work: Find a dimension in your warehouse and name its natural key and its surrogate key.
Ask which of your dimension attributes would change an old report if overwritten.

reels.title: One rider, three versions

beats.say: Rider 42 changes city twice. How many rows does the dimension need?
Three. Each has the same natural key, 42, but its own surrogate key: 1001, 1002, 1003. Each row also carries a valid from and a valid to date.
A trip on February fifth stores key 1001 in the fact table. That is the version true that day. The join is a plain equality on one column.

The alternative is an as-of join. Keep only the natural key plus dates, and join where the trip date falls between valid from and valid to. No extra key, but the join is heavier and easier to get wrong.

show.title: As-of join
items: Fact stores rider id 42 and trip date
Match the version where date is between valid from and valid to

check.q: Why does the fact table store the surrogate key rather than only the natural key?
opts: It points at the exact version true when the trip happened
check.why: The surrogate key identifies one version, so the fact joins to the attributes that were true at the time with a simple equality.

work: Sketch an SCD2 table for one dimension with three versions and valid from and to dates.
Write the as-of join for it and compare it with the surrogate key join.

reels.title: Shared, reused and packed dimensions

beats.say: Trips, payments and support tickets all report by city. Why do the numbers still sometimes disagree?
Because each team defined city differently. A conformed dimension fixes that: one shared dim city, used by every fact, so metrics line up.
A role-playing dimension is one date table used three times in the trip fact: request date, pickup date and payment date. Same table, three roles.

A junk dimension packs flags like airport, shared and scheduled into one small table of combinations, instead of ten columns. A degenerate dimension is just the trip id sitting in the fact, with no table of its own.

show.title: Keeping the fact tidy
items: Junk dimension: flag combinations in one small table
Fact holds one key, not ten flags
Degenerate dimension: trip id lives in the fact

check.q: A trip fact has request, pickup and payment dates. Which pattern is this?
check.why: One dim date table is used in several roles by the same fact.

work: List the dimensions that two of your facts both use and check they are truly the same table.
Find a fact with many boolean flags and consider a junk dimension.

reels.title: Mini-dimensions, bridges and the unknown member

beats.say: A rider's rating changes weekly. Do you add a new row to a ten million row dimension every time?

show.sub: A new row for every rating change?

beats.say: No. Split fast-changing things like rating band and loyalty tier into a small mini-dimension. The big table stays stable, and the fact points at both.
A trip can use two promo codes. A bridge table links trips to promos with a weight, say fifty percent each, so revenue is not counted twice.
And if a trip's driver is not loaded yet, give it key minus one, the unknown member. The row still joins and is not silently dropped.

check.q: Why does a bridge table carry a weight?
opts: So a measure split across many promos adds up once, not twice
check.why: Without weights, joining a trip to two promos repeats the fare and totals double count.

work: Find an attribute that changes weekly in a big dimension and test a mini-dimension for it.
Check that every dimension has a minus one unknown row.

reels.title: Where these patterns bite

beats.say: Why did your revenue drop after you joined trips to drivers?
An inner join drops trips whose driver row is missing. That is a late arriving dimension. Point those facts at unknown member minus one, and repair them when the driver row lands.
Bridge tables bite the other way. Join a trip to two promos and the fare appears twice. Multiply by the weight, and make sure weights sum to one.
Conformed dimensions break when one team changes a definition alone. And an SCD2 join must filter on dates, or one trip matches every version of the rider.

show.title: More gotchas
items: SCD2 as-of join needs the date filter
Without it, one trip matches every version

check.q: After joining trips to an SCD2 rider table without a date condition, trip counts rise. Why?
opts: Each trip matches every version of its rider
The surrogate key is duplicated in the fact
check.why: Without the valid from and valid to filter, a trip matches all versions of the rider and rows multiply.

work: Add a test that fact row counts match before and after each dimension join.
Report how many facts point at key minus one each day.

reels.title: Do you still need surrogate keys?

beats.say: Do you really need surrogate keys in a lakehouse?
Surrogate keys make joins simple and fast, and shield you when source ids change or merge. But they force load order: dimension first, then facts, with a key lookup on every load.
As-of joins on natural key and dates skip the lookup, so facts load on their own. The cost is range joins on huge tables, which are slower and harder to prune.

show.title: As-of join trade-off
items: Good for streaming and late data

beats.say: I would pick surrogate keys for large, stable, widely shared dimensions, and as-of joins for streaming or fast-moving data. I would add a mini-dimension only under heavy churn, because it adds a join.

check.q: Which setup favors an as-of join on natural key over surrogate keys?
opts: A huge, stable, shared dim customer
A streaming pipeline where facts arrive before dimensions
A report that needs the fastest possible joins
check.why: As-of joins remove the load order and key lookup, so facts can land independently of the dimension.

work: Measure join time for a surrogate key join and an as-of join on your largest fact.
Document which dimensions use which approach and why.

reels.title: The shoebox of receipts

beats.say: Imagine a shoebox full of receipts. Before you sort anything, what does one receipt actually stand for?

show.text: What does one row stand for?
show.sub: Think of a shoebox of receipts

beats.say: That is the grain: one sentence saying what one row means. Say, one receipt per coffee bought. Decide this first, because everything else depends on it.
Each receipt has labels that describe it: which cashier, which shop, which day. Those are dimensions. It also has numbers you can add up, like price and cups. Those are facts.

chip.text: Facts are numbers you add up

beats.say: Keep every label on one flat card per shop, and you have a star. Split the card into city, then country, then region, and you have a snowflake.

check.q: In the receipt analogy, which is the grain?
opts: The shop name printed on each receipt
The sentence 'one receipt per coffee bought'
The total price of all receipts
check.why: The grain is the plain-words statement of what one row means. Shop is a dimension and price is a fact.

work: Pick one table you own and write its grain as one sentence.
List which columns are labels (dimensions) and which are numbers (facts).

reels.title: Four steps, one star

beats.say: A rider taps once, and a trip happens. How do you turn that into a clean table? Four steps, always in the same order.

Step one, pick the business process: completing a trip, not a department. Step two, declare the grain: one row per completed trip. If a city does two million trips a day, that is two million rows a day.

show.title: Process, then grain
items: 2. Grain: one row per completed trip
Two million trips a day = two million rows

beats.say: Step three, dimensions: rider, driver, city, date, payment method. Each becomes a small table joined by a key. Step four, facts: fare, distance, minutes, measured at exactly the trip grain.
Now revenue by city by month needs fact_trip joined to dim_city and dim_date. Two joins, one hop each. That is a star.

check.q: What must you settle immediately after choosing the business process?
opts: The grain: what one row means
check.why: Grain is step two. Dimensions and facts only make sense once you know exactly what one row represents.

work: Walk a new model through all four steps in order before writing any SQL.
Estimate rows per day at your declared grain to sanity-check size.

reels.title: When the grain gets mixed

beats.say: Your revenue number is double what finance reports. What went wrong? Very often, the grain was mixed.
Say fact_trip is one row per completed trip, but someone adds a row per leg of a shared ride. Now a twenty dollar fare repeats on three rows, and a sum says sixty.
The fix is one grain per fact table. Put legs in their own fact table, and keep the fare at trip level. Every fact must be true at the declared grain.

show.title: Rules that prevent it
items: Legs get their own fact table
Fare lives only at trip grain

beats.say: Snowflakes add another trap. Country sits three joins from the fact, so every query pays for them, and one missing key under an inner join silently drops rows.

check.q: A fact table has a fare on every row, but rows are per ride leg while fare is per trip. What breaks?
check.why: A trip-level number repeated on several leg rows is counted once per leg when summed.

work: Check each fact column is valid at the table's stated grain.
Test that row counts do not change after joining to each dimension.

reels.title: Star by default, snowflake by proof

beats.say: When would you ever choose a snowflake over a star? Rarely, and you should be able to say why.
Snowflaking saves storage by keeping country once. But on columnar engines a repeated country column compresses to almost nothing. Storage is cheap. Extra joins and analyst time are not.
A snowflake earns its place for a huge shared hierarchy that changes often, like a fifty million item catalogue, or when a regulated reference table needs a single owner.
So default to stars with conformed dimensions shared across facts. Snowflake only for a measured reason, or keep it normalised underneath and publish a flat view.

check.q: Why is the storage saving of a snowflake weak on a columnar warehouse?
opts: Repeated column values compress very well
check.why: Columnar storage compresses repeated values heavily, so flat dimensions cost little while snowflake joins still cost query time.

work: Default new marts to stars and require a measured reason for any snowflake.
Share conformed dimensions such as date and city across fact tables.

reels.title: The index card for every customer

beats.say: How does a shop spot its regulars without rereading five years of receipts every single night?

show.sub: There must be a cheaper way

beats.say: Give each customer one index card. On it, write every date they visited. Each night, take yesterday's cards and just add today's visits. The giant receipt box stays closed.
A brand new customer gets a fresh card with one date. Someone who skipped today keeps their card exactly as it was. A list of dates kept inside one card is what engineers call an array.
So one glance at a card tells you if they came this week or this month. Fast, cheap, and no digging. That is a cumulative table.

check.q: Why does the shop update yesterday's cards instead of reading all receipts?
opts: Adding one day to a card is far cheaper than rereading all history
Cards are more accurate than receipts
check.why: The card already holds the past, so each night only today's small change is processed.

work: Find one daily job at work that rescans all history and ask if yesterday's output could be reused.
Explain a cumulative table to a non-technical colleague using the index card idea.

reels.title: Array, struct and map

beats.say: Why would a database column hold more than one value?

An array holds an ordered list, like recent active dates. A struct groups related fields, like fare 120.5 and distance 8.2 kilometres, in one value. A map holds key value pairs, like surge 1.4 and promo 0.1.
A map suits sparse attributes, where each row has different keys, so you avoid fifty mostly empty columns. A struct keeps a nested event together as one unit.
The payoff is that one row can carry its own history or detail, with no extra join table. That is the base for cumulative design.

show.text: One row carries its own history

check.q: Which type best fits attributes that differ from row to row, like surge and promo?
check.why: A map stores only the keys a row has, avoiding many mostly empty columns.

work: List wide tables at work with many null columns and consider a map.
Check which of your engines supports array, struct and map natively.

reels.title: Building today from yesterday

beats.say: Can you build today's table from yesterday's table instead of all history?

Yes. Take yesterday's table, say a million riders, each with a list of active dates. Take today's activity, maybe three hundred thousand riders. Join them with a full outer join, which keeps rows from both sides even without a match.

show.title: *Full outer join* of two small inputs

beats.say: Active rider: put today's date at the front of their list. Inactive rider: list unchanged. Rider seen for the first time: a new row with a one item list.
Today you read two inputs, not years of events. The cost per day stays flat even as history grows.

show.sub: Two inputs, not years of events

check.q: Why a full outer join, not an inner join, to build today's table?
opts: To keep inactive riders from yesterday and add brand new riders
To drop riders who were inactive
check.why: Inactive riders exist only yesterday and new riders only today. A full outer join keeps both.

work: Write the full outer join on paper for one entity and its three outcomes.
Estimate rows read today with this design versus a full history scan.

reels.title: Reading state from the list

beats.say: What can you learn from one row holding a list of dates?
Daily active: is today in the list. Weekly active: any date in the last seven days. Monthly active: any date in the last thirty. No scan of raw events at all.

show.title: Derived from the list
items: Daily: today is in the list
Weekly: any date in last 7 days
Monthly: any date in last 30 days

beats.say: Growth accounting gives each rider a state. New: first active today. Retained: active yesterday and today. Churned: active yesterday, not today. Resurrected: was inactive, now active again.
A rider whose newest date is ten twenty, seen again on ten twenty one, is retained. If the newest date is ten seventeen, there was a gap, so that rider is resurrected.

check.q: A rider's newest stored date is 10-17 and they are active on 10-21. Their state is:
check.why: They were inactive for days, had earlier activity, and are now back, which is resurrected.

work: Define new, retained, churned and resurrected in SQL on your own user table.
Replace one weekly active scan of raw events with a lookup on the date list.

reels.title: When the chain breaks

beats.say: Your cumulative table has a bug on day forty. What happens on day four hundred?
It is still there. Each day is built from the previous day, so errors flow forward. The fix is to rebuild from the last known good day, replaying every day after it, in order.
That is also why backfills cannot run in parallel. Day ten needs day nine finished first. A year of backfill means three hundred sixty five sequential runs.

show.sub: Day N needs day N minus 1

beats.say: Watch the full outer join. A missing side gives nulls, so coalesce the key and treat a null list as empty. And lists grow forever, so cap them or drop riders inactive for a long time.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Cap list or prune dormant riders

check.q: A bug is found on day 40 of a 400 day cumulative table. What is the fix?
opts: Rebuild from the last good day, running each day in order
check.why: Later days inherited the bad state, and each day needs the previous one, so replay sequentially.

work: Keep a known good snapshot every month so rebuilds start close to the bug.
Add a null and duplicate-date check to the daily job.

reels.title: Why a rerun can corrupt history

beats.say: What if the job for today runs twice?
If it reads yesterday's partition and writes today's partition, the rerun gives the same answer. Safe.
But if it updates one table in place, today's date is added twice, and every later day inherits the damage. Retention and churn counts then drift silently.

show.title: In place update, run twice
show.text:
run 1: [10-21, 10-20]
run 2: [10-21, 10-21, 10-20]
later days copy the duplicate

beats.say: So keep one partition per day, overwrite that partition, and never read the table you are writing. Dedupe dates before prepending. A late event for an old day means rebuilding that day and every day after it.

check.q: What makes a cumulative job safe to rerun?
opts: Reading day N minus 1 and overwriting only day N
check.why: Fixed input and overwritten output give the same result however many times it runs.

work: Check your job writes by overwriting a dated partition, not appending.
Add a test that no date appears twice in any list.

reels.title: Should you build it at all?

beats.say: When is a cumulative table the wrong choice?

It shines for long lived entity questions: retention, resurrection, days since last active. If you only need yesterday's active count, a plain daily aggregate from events is simpler, with no chain of dependencies.

The cost is storage that grows per entity, and a chain that forces sequential backfills. Cap the list at ninety days, or store a bit mask in one integer, where each bit is a day. Thirty one days fit in a thirty two bit integer.

show.title: Keep it bounded
items: Bit mask: one bit per day

beats.say: Alternatives: partitioned event scans with pruning when data is small, or slowly changing dimensions when you need attribute history with validity ranges. Choose cumulative when scans would be huge and the same questions repeat daily.

check.q: You only need yesterday's total active users and data is modest. Best choice?
opts: A cumulative table with date arrays
A simple daily aggregate over partitioned events
check.why: No long entity history is needed, so a plain aggregate avoids the dependency chain and backfill cost.

work: List your repeated entity-level questions and see which truly need history per entity.
Decide a cap or bit mask size and a pruning rule before launch.

reels.title: The address book that remembers

beats.say: If your friend moves house, should every old letter you sent be relabeled with their new address?

Of course not. A good address book keeps every address, with the dates they lived there. Each line says: from this day until that day, this address. That is a type two slowly changing dimension. A dimension is just the descriptive facts about something.
Now someone asks: where did Sam live when I sent the March letter? You find the line whose dates cover March. That is an as-of lookup. The current address is simply the line with no end date yet.
So old letters keep their true story, and new letters get the new one. History stays honest.

check.q: Sam moved in June. Which address belongs to a letter sent in March?
opts: The newest address, since it is current
The address whose date range covers March
check.why: An as-of lookup picks the version valid on the event date. Using the current address would rewrite history.

work: Pick one dimension you own and list which attributes someone might ask about as they were then.
Check whether your current dimension keeps old values or overwrites them.

reels.title: Backfill with the streak trick

beats.say: You have one row per rider per day, three hundred rows saying free, free, free. How do you squash that into a few rows with start and end dates?
First, flag a change. Put one if today's tier differs from yesterday's, otherwise zero. The very first day counts as one.
Next, take a running sum of those flags. That number is the streak. It holds steady while the tier holds steady, and goes up by one at every change.

Group by rider and streak. Each group is one version, with its first date as the start. Free, then plus, then free gives three rows, not two. Group by tier alone and the two free runs would merge, erasing the upgrade.

check.q: A rider goes free, plus, free. Why group by rider and streak instead of rider and tier?
opts: Grouping by tier merges the two free runs into one row
Streak is required by the warehouse
check.why: The streak increases at every change, so the two free runs get different numbers and stay separate versions.

work: Write the backfill with a lag comparison, a running sum, then a group by, and test it on a rider who returns to an earlier value.
Handle the first day per key so it counts as a change.

reels.title: The nightly incremental load

beats.say: Every night you receive a snapshot of two million drivers, but only two thousand changed. How do you update history without rewriting it all?

Compare today's snapshot with the current rows only, not the whole history. That sorts everything into five piles: old history untouched, current rows unchanged, changed rows to close, their new open versions, and brand-new keys.

Closing a row means setting its end date to today. In a warehouse, a merge closes the old rows, then an insert adds the new versions. Run both in one transaction, so a crash never leaves a closed row with no replacement.
Finally, make it idempotent. Run the same day twice and no rows are added, because the second run finds no differences against the current rows.

check.q: The nightly job is accidentally run twice for the same day. What should happen?
opts: The second run adds no rows
check.why: After the first run, current rows already match the snapshot, so the comparison finds no changes and nothing is added.

work: Compare snapshots to current rows only, never the full history table.
Run the merge and insert in one transaction.
Rerun a day in a test and assert the row count does not change.

reels.title: Why is_current gives wrong revenue

beats.say: Your revenue by tier report says plus riders bring in the most money. Why might it be wrong, and grow more wrong every month?

Joining trips to the dimension on is current gives every trip the rider's tier today. A rider who was free in March and upgraded in June has their March trips relabeled as plus. More riders change over time, so the error grows.
The fix is an as-of join. Match on the rider key, and require the trip date to be on or after valid from, and before valid to.
Use a half-open window. A trip on the exact change day then lands in exactly one row. If both ends are inclusive, that trip matches two rows and its revenue is counted twice.

show.title: Window edges
items: Both inclusive double counts the change day

check.q: Why does joining facts to the dimension on is_current distort revenue by tier?
opts: It drops rows with no match
It assigns today's tier to past trips
It counts the change day twice
check.why: is_current has one row per key, the latest, so all history is labeled with today's attributes.

work: Replace any is_current joins on historical facts with as-of joins.
Add a test that each fact row matches exactly one dimension row.
Use half-open validity windows everywhere.

reels.title: Late-arriving dimensions

beats.say: A trip arrives for driver 912, but the driver table has never heard of 912. Do you drop the trip?
No. Insert an inferred member: the driver id, with everything else marked unknown. Now the trip loads with a valid key and the revenue is not lost.
When the real driver record arrives, update that placeholder in place. The unknown row was never a true state of the driver, so it should not become a history version.
The trap: if the load treats the real record as a normal change, it closes the placeholder and adds a second row. Monitor how many inferred members stay unknown for days.

check.q: A trip arrives before its driver exists in the dimension. What is the best handling?
opts: Drop the trip until the driver arrives
Insert an inferred member, then update it later
Point the trip to the first driver row
check.why: An inferred member keeps the key valid and the fact loaded, and the real record later fills it in.

work: Add an inferred flag column to your dimension.
Write a check that lists inferred members older than one day.

reels.title: When SCD2 is the wrong tool

beats.say: Should every dimension be type two? Not at all. History has a price in rows, joins, and complexity.
Take driver location changing hourly. One million drivers times twenty-four changes is twenty-four million new rows every day. The dimension stops being small, and every as-of join gets slower.
Better options: overwrite with type one when nobody needs the past, like fixing a typo. Put fast-changing values on the fact table. Or split them into a small mini-dimension of banded values.

show.title: Instead choose
items: Fast values live on the fact

beats.say: If queries are rare and storage is cheap, plain daily snapshots can win on simplicity. SCD2 wins when changes are rare and as-of queries are common. Ask: will anyone need the value as it was, and how often does it change?

check.q: Driver location changes hourly and nobody queries old locations. What do you choose?
opts: Overwrite or keep it on the fact table
check.why: SCD2 would create millions of rows for a value no one needs historically. Overwriting or storing it on the fact is far cheaper.

work: Estimate daily new rows per attribute as keys times change rate before choosing type two.
Decide per column, not per table, which attributes need history.

reels.title: Pins and string: what a graph is

beats.say: How would you find every friend of a friend of yours, without asking each person one by one?
Picture a wall covered in pins and string. Each pin is a thing, like a person or a driver. Each string is a relationship, like referred or rated. Pins are called vertices. Strings are called edges.
To find friends of friends, you start at your pin and follow the strings twice. You are not adding up totals. You are walking connections.
And a new kind of relationship, like shares a phone, needs no new wall. You just tie a different coloured string.

show.kicker: Just a new kind of string

check.q: In a graph model, what is an edge?
opts: A thing such as a rider or driver
A total such as revenue per city
check.why: Vertices are the things; edges are the relationships connecting them, such as referred or rated.

work: List three questions your team asks that are about connections, not totals.
Sketch those questions as pins and strings on a whiteboard.

reels.title: Two tables hold a whole network

beats.say: How do you store an entire network in just two plain tables?

One table holds vertices: an identifier like rider colon one, a type, and a map of properties, such as city Pune. The other holds edges: a subject, an object, an edge type, and properties. For example, rider one referred rider two on April fourteenth.
Because the schema is generic, a new relationship type is just a new value in the edge type column. No new table and no migration.

show.title: Why generic works
items: New relationship equals new edge type value

beats.say: To ask who rider one referred, then who those people referred, you use a recursive query. It starts with rider one's edges, then joins the edges table to its own results, once per hop. Two hops means two joins.

check.q: A team wants to add a new relationship called shares_device. What does the generic schema need?
opts: A new edges table for that relationship
A new edge type value in the existing edges table
A new column on every vertex
check.why: Edges carry a type column, so a new relationship is simply new rows with a new type value.

work: Write a recursive query that finds referrals up to two hops from one rider.
Check what indexes exist on subject and object in your edges table.

reels.title: Cycles and supernodes

beats.say: What happens if rider A refers rider B, and B refers A?
The recursive query never finishes. It walks A to B to A forever, and the rows keep growing. Two fixes: stop at a maximum depth, say five hops, or keep a visited set so you never revisit a vertex.

show.title: Fixing cycles
items: Depth limit, for example five hops
Visited set, never revisit a vertex
Without either, the query loops forever

beats.say: The second trap is the supernode: one vertex with millions of edges, like a promo code that every rider used. Any traversal touching it explodes, because one hop fans out into millions of rows.

chip.text: One hop becomes millions of rows

beats.say: So you cap the fan out, sample its edges, or skip that vertex in the traversal. Otherwise one hub turns a cheap query into an hours-long job.

show.text: Cap, sample or skip the hub

check.q: Your recursive referral query never finishes on real data. What is the most likely cause and fix?
opts: A cycle in the data; add a depth limit or visited set
Too few columns; add a properties map
The edges table is too small; add rows
check.why: Cycles such as A refers B refers A make the recursion loop forever unless depth is limited or visited vertices are tracked.

work: Add a depth limit to every recursive graph query you own.
Count edges per vertex and list the top ten supernodes.

reels.title: When SQL stops being enough

beats.say: When should you stop answering graph questions in SQL?
Recursive queries are fine for two or three hops on a warehouse you already run. But each hop is a self join, so cost grows with fan out, and deep traversal gets slow.

Move to Neo4j, Neptune or GraphFrames when you need many hops, shortest paths, community detection for fraud rings, or answers in milliseconds. A graph store follows pointers instead of joining tables.

show.title: Reach for a graph engine when

beats.say: The price is another system to run, load and keep in sync. If your questions are sums by category, stay dimensional. Choose graph only when relationships are the question.

chip.text: Sync, ops and cost to maintain

check.q: Which need most clearly justifies a dedicated graph engine over recursive SQL?
opts: Interactive fraud ring detection across many hops
check.why: Deep multi-hop traversal, community detection and interactive speed are where graph engines beat repeated self joins.

work: Measure how many hops your slowest graph question really needs.
Prototype the question in SQL first and note where latency breaks down.
Estimate sync and operating cost before proposing a graph database.

reels.title: The address book that remembers

beats.say: Your friend moves from Leeds to Bristol. Do you scratch out the old address in your book, or keep both?
Scratching it out is called overwrite. It is simple, but the past is gone. Old birthday cards you sent to Leeds now look like they went to Bristol.

Keeping both means adding a new line with dates. Leeds until March, Bristol since. Now every card matches where your friend lived then. That is a slowly changing dimension: a detail about a thing, like a rider's plan, that changes now and then, and you choose how much history to keep.
You choose per detail. Keep the birthday forever, overwrite typos, track addresses.

check.q: Why would you keep a new dated line instead of overwriting a friend's address?
opts: Old events still match where the friend lived at the time
It makes the book faster to write
check.why: Overwriting rewrites the past. Dated lines let old events be explained with the value that was true then.

work: List the attributes in one dimension you own and mark which ones people ask about historically.
Find one report whose old numbers changed after an attribute was overwritten.

reels.title: Type 2: one row per version

beats.say: A rider upgrades to Plus on October third, then drops back to free on October fourteenth. How does one rider end up with two rows?

Type 2 never edits history. When the tier changes, the pipeline closes the old row by setting its valid to date, then inserts a new row with a fresh surrogate key, which is just an id the warehouse makes up. Rider four gets key seven, then key eight.

show.title: dim_rider_tier
show.text:
rider_key rider_id tier valid_from valid_to  is_current
7         4        plus 2026-10-03 2026-10-14 false
8         4        free 2026-10-14 NULL       true
show.note: Close the old row, insert the new one

beats.say: Intervals are half open. Valid from is included, valid to is excluded. So October fourteenth belongs only to key eight, and a report for any date matches exactly one row.
The open row has a null valid to and current true, so today's queries simply filter on the flag.

check.q: With valid_from <= d < valid_to, which row owns October 14 in the example?
check.why: Key 7 ends exclusive at October 14, so that date falls only inside key 8's interval.

work: Write the as-of join for one fact table using valid_from <= event_date < valid_to.
Check your SCD tables use half-open intervals, not between.

reels.title: Picking an SCD type per column

beats.say: There are six SCD types, but you rarely pick one for a whole table. Which one fits which column?
Type zero keeps the original forever, like signup date. Type one overwrites, good for typo fixes. Type two adds rows, for city, tier or plan, anything a report must show as it was then.

Type three keeps current and previous in two columns, handy for one reorganisation. Type four keeps only the current row in the dimension and puts history in another table, for wide or fast changing data.
Type six is type two rows plus a current value column on every row, so one query can show the then-value and the now-value together.

show.sub: then-value and now-value in one query

check.q: Which type fits a report that must group by a rider's tier at the time of the trip and also by their tier today?
check.why: Type 6 keeps versioned rows plus a current-value column on each, so both views come from one query.

work: Annotate each column in a key dimension with its SCD type.
Document why each Type 1 column is safe to overwrite.

reels.title: Where SCD 2 bugs hide

beats.say: Your report says a rider was Plus on October fourteenth, but they were already free. Where did that bug come from?

Often from closed intervals. If valid to is inclusive and the next valid from is the same date, that day matches two rows and counts double. If valid to is a day early, it matches none. Half open intervals fix both.
Also guard the current row. Two rows flagged current for one rider will duplicate every join, so add a test that each natural key has exactly one.
And facts must use the version in force at event time. A late arriving change means re-cutting the intervals, and fixing surrogate keys on facts already loaded.

show.title: Late arriving changes
items: Join on event date, not today

check.q: Valid_to is inclusive and equals the next row's valid_from. What happens on that boundary date?
opts: It matches two rows and double counts
check.why: Both the closing and the opening row include that date, so a join returns two matches.

work: Add a test that each natural key has exactly one current row and no overlapping intervals.
Add a test for gaps between consecutive versions of the same key.
Plan how late arriving changes will be backfilled.

reels.title: When Type 2 is the wrong call

beats.say: Type 2 everywhere sounds safe. So why do big teams avoid it?

show.sub: safe on paper, costly at scale

beats.say: A fast changing column, like a driver's last seen location, adds a row per change. A ten million row dimension can balloon into billions, and every fact join gets slower. That is when you use type four: a small current table, with history pushed to a side table.
If only a few reports need history, a daily snapshot of the dimension may be simpler than merge logic. Type six costs more, since every old row is rewritten whenever the current value changes.
Default to type two for business critical attributes, type one for the rest, and decide per column with the analyst who asks the question.

check.q: A column changes thousands of times a day and few reports need its history. What is the best default?
opts: Type 4 or a snapshot, keeping the main dimension small
check.why: Type 2 on a fast column inflates the dimension and slows every join. Separating history keeps joins cheap.

work: Measure row growth per column in your Type 2 dimensions and flag the fast ones.
Compare daily snapshots against merge logic for a dimension with few history consumers.
